drills.q: A pod is permanently Pending; its PVC shows Bound. What's the likely cause and the fix?
drills.a: volumeBindingMode defaulted to Immediate, so the PV was bound to a zone before the pod was scheduled; the scheduler later placed the pod in a different zone the volume can't attach to. Fix: delete and recreate the PVC against a StorageClass set to WaitForFirstConsumer so binding happens after scheduling.

drills.q: A security reviewer pulls a Secret's YAML via kubectl and reads the plaintext password instantly. Is this a bug in Kubernetes, or expected behavior?
drills.a: Expected — Secrets are base64-encoded by default, not encrypted, and base64 is trivially reversible. This is exactly why EncryptionConfiguration with a real provider must be explicitly configured for actual confidentiality; the default is not a bug, it's the well-documented (and frequently missed) baseline.

drills.q: You just enabled EncryptionConfiguration with a KMS provider on a cluster that's been running for two years with hundreds of existing Secrets. Are you done?
drills.a: No — only newly written/updated objects get encrypted going forward. All existing Secrets remain in their prior (base64-only) form until explicitly rewritten. The rollout needs a follow-up bulk rewrite pass (get + replace every existing Secret) to actually bring them under the new encryption.

drills.q: A team updates a ConfigMap and expects a running Deployment's pods to pick up the new value within a minute, but nothing changes even after an hour. What's the most likely explanation?
drills.a: The value is being injected via an env var (envFrom/valueFrom.configMapKeyRef), which is captured once at pod start and never updates for that pod's lifetime, unlike a volume mount which syncs live via kubelet's periodic sync. Fix: force a rollout, commonly via a checksum annotation on the pod template tied to the ConfigMap's content.

drills.q: An incident review finds a ServiceAccount token exfiltrated from a compromised pod six months ago still works today. What K8s version-era behavior explains this, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Pre-1.24 default behavior: ServiceAccounts auto-generated a long-lived Secret-based token with no built-in expiry, mounted into every pod using it. Fix: migrate to 1.24+ bound tokens via the TokenRequest API (time-limited, audience-bound, object-bound to the pod's lifetime) and delete any lingering legacy long-lived Secret tokens.

drills.q: A pentest finds a namespace-scoped ServiceAccount effectively has cluster-admin-level access despite its Role looking narrowly scoped to 'create tokens.' Explain the escalation path.
drills.a: The Role grants create access on serviceaccounts/token for a different, highly-privileged ServiceAccount. Anyone with that permission can mint a fresh bound token impersonating the privileged ServiceAccount at will — functionally equivalent to holding all of that ServiceAccount's permissions directly, even though the Role itself lists only a narrow-sounding verb.

drills.q: Why might disabling automountServiceAccountToken cluster-wide as a blanket security hardening pass break production, and how should it actually be rolled out?
drills.a: Any workload that genuinely calls the Kubernetes API (operators, controllers, client-go-based tooling) breaks outright with no token to authenticate with. It should be rolled out per-workload after auditing (via API server access logs or similar) which ServiceAccounts actually make API requests, setting automountServiceAccountToken: false only on the ones confirmed not to need it.

drills.q: A team wants a RWX PVC on their default cloud block-storage StorageClass and provisioning fails. Why, and what's the real fix?
drills.a: Most common block-storage CSI drivers (e.g. AWS EBS) only support ReadWriteOnce, not ReadWriteMany. Concurrent multi-node mounts need a genuinely different storage backend (EFS, Azure Files, NFS-backed StorageClass) with real performance/consistency tradeoffs versus block storage — RWX isn't something every StorageClass can be configured to support.
